paragraphs: The first to raise a torch was a boy from the Xianbei left cavalry. He planted it in the middle of the road, lifted a bloodstained hand, and screamed himself hoarse: “Helai Yan is dead!”

From the camp gate to the western palisade, tents sprang alight one after another. Men pulled on armor or snatched up bows; some ran barefoot into the wet mud without even putting on their boots. Names from the old Yan army—the Left Valiant Cavalry, the Changli Horsemen, the Murong household troops—rose out of the tumult. Their banners had been surrendered half a month earlier. The old names remained on every tongue, and at one call each man knew where he belonged.

The Di soldiers were gathering too. Word spread that Liang Hu’s knife, its wolf-fang pattern unmistakable, had been found beneath the dead man. Others said the Xianbei meant to seize Fu Chong before dawn. Every retelling acquired another detail. By the time the rumor reached the eastern stables, it had become: “The Yan men killed a sentry and are marching on headquarters.”
Liang Hu stood at the mouth of his tent. Eyes watched him from every side. Sweat soaked the empty sheath at his waist.
“When did it go missing?” Zhao An asked under his breath.
“It was there after supper.”
“Who came in?”

Liang Hu shook his head. A laborer had come to mend the sleeping mats, soldiers to collect rations, carters to deliver firewood. People had gone in and out all evening; how could he remember them all? His lips drained of color. Suddenly he started toward the camp road.
Zhao An caught his arm. “If you go over there now, they won’t listen.”
“And they’ll listen if I hide?”

Manu braced him from behind and poured out a frantic stream of Qiang speech. Liang Hu understood none of it. Zhai Hei dragged out a wooden shield and planted it before the four of them. The tent in which five men had quarreled over their places that afternoon had become a little besieged fortress.

When they carried in the door plank, the dead man’s new uniform had gone black with blood. A soldier recognized the scar on Helai Yan’s face, dropped to his knees, took the muddy hand, and wept. Murong Shao forced his way through the crowd, seized the short knife with the wolf-fang carving, and raised it toward the Di ranks.
“Take a good look at your knife!”

The Xianbei in front drew steel. At once the Di leveled their spears. The thirty paces between them shrank by half under the pressure of the crowd. Someone struck an opposing helmet with the back of his blade; a retaliatory spear opened an arm. As the first blood from a living man hit the camp road, hundreds of torches tilted forward together.

Murong Chui reached the wooden platform before he had fastened his cloak. He ordered the halt drums beaten. Their rhythm rolled down the road, but only the Han troops at the outer edge withdrew a few steps. Hearing old comrades address him as the Prince of Wu, the Xianbei pressed toward the platform demanding vengeance. The Di answered by shouting Fu Chong’s name.
Murong Chui surveyed the surging firelight. For a moment his hand stayed motionless on his sword.
“Helai Yan was my soldier,” he said.

Cheers answered him. He raised a hand to cut them off. “That is precisely why his death in the First Battalion must be investigated under the First Battalion’s law. Whoever takes private revenge for him will answer to me first.”
“We’ve found the knife!” Murong Shao shouted.
“Have you found the man who used it?”
Murong Shao hesitated, then thrust the hilt still higher. “Liang Hu!”
“Bring him here.”

Liang Hu emerged from the Di line of his own accord. Zhao An followed, with Manu and Zhai Hei guarding either side. Near the plank bearing the body, a stone narrowly missed his head. Murong Chui ordered the guards to interpose their shields and bring him onto the platform.
“Is this your knife?”
“Yes.”
“Did you kill Helai Yan?”
“No.”
“Who stole it?”
“I don’t know.”

The crowd jeered. Liang Hu clamped his jaw shut. After studying him, Murong Chui ordered the military magistrate to seal the knife as evidence and hold the man in headquarters, beyond anyone else’s reach. Further questioning would yield none of the answer needed tonight. A knife could kill one man; placed in the proper hands, it could be used to kill thirty thousand.

Fu Chong arrived with his household guards. Three hundred suits of old Di armor emerged together from the dark, copper wolf-fang fittings flashing in the firelight. The Di soldiers seemed relieved by the familiar armor. The Xianbei tightened their fingers on bowstrings, and even their sobbing subsided.
“The Champion General arrests a Di man while letting Yan soldiers form a mob?” Fu Chong demanded. “Detain their captains first. Then you can hold an inquiry.”
“The Di are forming a mob as well,” Murong Chui said.
“They’re defending themselves against an assault.”
Murong Chui pointed toward the body. “Was Helai Yan defending himself when he died?”
Fu Chong’s face hardened. “You suspect me?”
“I haven’t investigated you. I can see only that you’ve brought guards you were not authorized to bring.”

Fu Chong drew his sword halfway and forced it back into the sheath. Fu Hong arrived just then, pushing through the crowd. The two generals were nearly face to face, and their soldiers had weapons trained upon one another. In that instant the crown prince thought the acrimonious councils he chaired at the Secretariat had been as gentle as family dinners.

He had messengers repeat the order to secure the gates, carry away the injured, and keep every company in its place. He ordered Han infantry with shields between the first opposing ranks. Almost no one stepped back. Each soldier watched the captain he knew, waiting for him to move first.
“Your Highness sees it now?” Fu Chong murmured to Fu Hong. “What use are military magistrates to troops who won’t recognize their commanders?”
Before Fu Hong could answer, hoofbeats rang outside the gate. A patrol rider lay nearly flat across his horse, a short arrow buried in his shoulder. He reached the entrance and fell.

“The whole city says the First Battalion has rebelled!” he gasped as men lifted him. “They say the Heavenly King is dying and the palace gates are sealed. Men are handing out blades in the West Market. Riders have gathered outside the princes' compounds…”

Not one report was confirmed; the arrow in his shoulder was real. At the words “the Heavenly King is dying,” the camp erupted like water at a boil. Some demanded to rush home to Chang’an and protect their families. Others claimed old Di ministers had seized the palace. Still others urged a breakout before the gates could close.

Fu Hong knelt beside the wounded rider and asked who had fired. The man had seen nothing in the dark. Asked where the rumor began, he named three or four different wards. Fu Hong stood and saw that the old line dividing the camp road had disappeared. Each side had bunched into a denser mass. Between them lay only a patch of mud trampled to pulp.

In the city, Fu Jian was receiving urgent reports in his night robe. The palace had not been closed; the Heavenly King was not ill. Yet rumor had already traveled around Chang’an ahead of him. Yao Chang came to request command of three thousand Right Guard soldiers to settle the disorder. He made a careful proposal, down to the ways he would separate the two forces and collect their weapons.
Fu Jian ordered a map spread out. “Where do your three thousand men come from?”
“Former Qiang units and forces of the capital district. All have been mixed according to the new decree.”
“Will the men in the camp recognize their old unit names?”
Yao Chang lowered his eyes. “Some of them will.”
“The Di and Xianbei already distrust everyone outside their own ranks. If you take three thousand familiar faces in among them, whom will they believe?”

Yao Chang did not argue further. Fu Jian turned to Quan Yi. “Call out two hundred Feathered Forest Guards. No personal contingents. All other camps are to stand fast, with explicit orders not to enter the city. Has the Duke of Yangping returned?”
“He arrived at dusk. His case files are still at the Secretariat.”
“Bring him with us.”

Quan Yi knelt to dissuade him: thirty thousand men waited beyond the walls, their temper unknowable. Fu Jian merely fastened his cloak. “Hong’er is still in there.” At that, no one in the chamber could pretend the Heavenly King was a man who could not be wounded.
Before mounting, he glanced back at Yao Chang, who stood under the eaves with his hands folded in his sleeves, tall and composed in the lamplight.
“I leave Chang’an’s ward gates in your care tonight, General Yao.”
“I obey Your Majesty.”
“If someone claims the palace is locked, take him to the gate and let him see. Don’t begin with the whip.”
Yao Chang bowed. Fu Jian had already ridden away. A mourning banner hanging from the palace eaves lifted in the night wind, then fell back into the light.

When the two hundred guards arrived, the halt drums had beaten several times. Still no company would withdraw first. Fu Jian rode between the banks of torches. Some old soldiers recognized him, yet gripped their weapons just as tightly. Dismounting, he saw the central Qin banner standing intact, though hidden from view behind thousands of men’s backs.
“Raise the banner where they can see it,” he told Fu Hong.

Fu Hong climbed the high platform with a dozen messengers. They tied fresh torches to the pole, lighting the black lettering wrinkled by the wind. Fu Jian ordered company officers to unbuckle their swords first and place them on a rack below the platform. Ordinary soldiers could keep their weapons but must retreat thirty paces; medical orderlies were to pass through the cleared road with the wounded.

Murong Chui surrendered his sword first. After a pause, Fu Chong removed his as well. Murong Shao still clutched the sealed wolf-fang knife. In full view of the camp, Fu Rong took it and gave it, seal and all, to the military magistrate, with one Di and one Xianbei clerk appointed to witness the custody. Only after Murong Shao saw one of his own men sign did he step back.
A Xianbei boy pulled a small old-Yan banner from inside his tunic and gripped it until his knuckles whitened. Fu Jian approached and noticed two lines of mending stitches at its corner.
“Who sewed it for you?”
“My mother. She said we couldn’t throw everything from the old camp away.”

Fu Jian gently rolled the little banner and handed it back. “Keep it under your coat. If you raise it tonight, the Di will go looking for their banners too. There’ll be no one left to bury Helai Yan.”
The boy stared, then tucked the banner back inside his clothes. Fu Jian moved on without ordering a search for the other men’s relics.

He mounted the wooden platform and ordered the drums to stop. When their relentless thunder ceased, coughing and weeping could be heard in the distance, along with the scrape of stretcher legs through the mud.
“I am still alive,” Fu Jian said.

Someone nearby laughed once, with terror in the sound. Messengers repeated his words farther out. The acclaim was ragged but finally drowned the rumor of his death. Fu Jian promised no captured killer. Instead he had Fu Rong bring out the findings and tell each company what was known: they knew whose knife it was; they did not know who had wielded it. Helai Yan’s murder must be investigated. Any killing committed tonight would be investigated too.
“To stab one man to death is murder,” Fu Jian said, looking from side to side. “To set an entire camp at war over that knife would destroy thirty thousand. Someone is waiting for you to begin.”

A voice cursed him: the dead man was Xianbei, and still the Heavenly King cared only about military law. Fu Jian found the speaker, an old soldier with white hair and beard. “Where is the dead man’s family? Does anyone know?”
“In Chang’an.”
“Then send his family the truth, not another reassuring lie. Fetch them to identify him. Don’t let his wife and daughter hear ten different accounts of his death before a messenger reaches them.”

The old soldier stood open-mouthed for a long while, then slowly lowered his blade. Officers began leading their men backward. The Han shields drew away first, followed by the Qiang archers. The Xianbei and Di faced each other longest. Only when Fu Hong had Helai Yan’s door-plank stretcher carried out of the middle did a narrow passage open, and the two sides begin retreating while watching one another. Narrow though it was, the road could carry the medical orderlies at last.
Liang Hu was detained that night, but not tortured. The inquiry began with his knife.

Fu Rong had only just returned from Ye; his clothes still held the dust of the road. He went first to the medical tent to examine the body. The stab below Helai Yan’s left breast was deep but had missed heart and lungs; a strong man might have walked some distance after it. A crushed place at the back of his skull was far more likely to have killed him. The cut across his left palm looked like a wound from grasping a bare blade. Coarse hemp fibers clung between his fingers; a few horsehairs lay among the grass clenched in his right fist.
“The knife wounded him. It may not have been what killed him,” Fu Rong said.
The surgeon measured the wound with his knuckles and looked up. “Yes.”

Fu Rong did not declare Liang Hu innocent. Liang Hu might still have used the knife; the other injuries could have been inflicted by the same person. He ordered them to trace Helai Yan’s last movements and determine when the blade had left Liang Hu’s sheath.

Zhao An testified that the knife was hanging from a tent post after supper. Liang Hu admitted he had quarreled with Helai Yan that afternoon, about an arrow case and the old kingdom neither knew how to discuss. Before leaving, Helai Yan had asked which side Liang Hu would stand on if the two peoples ever fought. Liang Hu said he would stand where he could stay alive.
“What did he say?” Fu Rong asked.
“He said he didn’t know either.” Liang Hu’s eyes reddened. “Then he left. That was all.”

Questioned about visitors, the men recalled a laborer mending mats, two soldiers delivering grain, and a thin-faced firewood carter with a black mole above his right eyebrow. Someone remembered the carter telling Helai Yan that General Murong now served the Di alone.

Fu Rong ordered the west-gate tally checked. The gate clerk initially insisted that no cart had passed out the previous night. By dusk he remembered a firewood cart bearing a construction-office token, with two laborers aboard. The construction office had issued no such dispatch.

At first light, they found the cart five li away beside a ruined earth-god shrine. The ox was gone. A bloody hemp rope, a wooden mallet, and bundles of undelivered firewood remained. Hair clung to the mallet, consistent with the head wound. Behind the shrine lay discarded straw sandals, their soles dark with mud like that in the western ditch. The track ran northward and divided into three near a water mill.

At the mill, a man climbing over the rear wall was shot in the leg and captured. He called himself Sun Fu, a man of Hedong. On him were ten taels of gold, a forged construction-office token, and a strip of old leather cut from Liang Hu’s scabbard.

Fu Rong asked how he knew Helai Yan. Sun Fu claimed the dead man had killed his elder brother. Asked in which year and battle, he could not answer. Fu Rong set the hemp rope and wooden mallet before him; sweat began to pour from his brow. When asked who had lured Helai Yan out of camp, he suddenly repeated only one sentence: “I want to see the Heavenly King.”

Fu Rong would not bargain for a confession with false promises. He said he would put the request to Fu Jian, who alone could grant it. Sun Fu’s eyes shifted; the answer seemed to frighten him more than threatened torture. At last he admitted stealing the knife from the tent, but insisted everything else was a private vendetta.

The military register soon showed that Sun Fu had been an archer in the Hedong Han units. Three years earlier he had assaulted a comrade and deserted. He knew camp procedure and the forms of official tokens. Fu Rong kept him out of the ordinary guard tents, under separate watch, and restricted his visitors. Still, the next disaster came.

In the afternoon, a medical attendant arrived at the makeshift military prison with a wooden pass, saying he had come to redress Sun Fu’s wounded leg. The guards checked the duty list: a healer called Chen Wu was indeed assigned. They let him in. Less than half an hour later Sun Fu began to convulse, his lips blackening. By the time the surgeon arrived, bitter medicinal dregs remained in his mouth, and he was dead.

The real Chen Wu had been in the casualty tent, seen by more than a dozen men. The visitor was an elderly man calling himself Zhou Liu, recently hired to transport medicines. The address he left, in Yongning Ward, belonged to a courtyard abandoned six months earlier. But his medical badge and clothes had been genuine. The question of authentic passes, which had vexed the new army on its first day, had now claimed a life.

Fu Jian examined the sealed medical pass himself and said nothing for a long time. Fu Rong reported the affair of the Ye registers: someone there had borrowed a genuine letter, used a genuine badge, and concealed illicit objects in an actual ordnance wagon. Now a killer had entered the camp with a genuine medical pass. The cases might be connected; evidence of who had joined them was still lacking.

Yao Chang came out from the city, heard the testimony, and asked whether Sun Fu had spoken a name before his death. Fu Rong shook his head. Yao Chang sighed. “To find the man who paid the money, it seems one must travel farther than the man who carried it.” Everyone understood the remark. It proved nothing against anyone.

Toward nightfall, guards seized a horse dealer outside the camp. He had tried to burn an old cart by the roadside; among the ashes lay a wooden box once used to hold gold, with a Chang’an money house’s mark under the lid. Shown Sun Fu’s body, the man trembled so violently he could scarcely speak. He admitted he was in debt; a gray-robed stranger had told him to find a deserter, deliver money, then destroy the cart. The stranger lacked the little finger on his right hand. They had arranged to meet in an abandoned house in Pingkang Ward. Fu Rong found only medicinal powder and charred fragments of wooden passes there.

The horse dealer was held for questioning. This time Fu Jian ordered four Feathered Forest Guards to watch him in rotation, with food and water inspected separately and no medical attendant admitted alone. Next morning, the seal on the prison door was intact, but the dealer hung dead from a wooden rail. The knot in his belt faced an odd direction. Faint red marks around his wrists suggested thin cords had bound them. The four guards told different stories: one had gone for charcoal; another had suffered stomach pains and been helped outside; the last two insisted they had not slept.
“Suicide? Or did someone get in?” Fu Jian asked.
Fu Rong knelt beside the corpse and carefully drew a hair-fine black thread from the man’s wrist.
“All we know now is that someone touched his hands before he died.” He folded the thread into a piece of paper. “The rest must be examined in Chang’an.”

Dusk fell again. The First Battalion lit its cooking fires on schedule. Liang Hu was released, though nobody cheered. He went into the medical tent and found Helai Yan washed clean of mud and blood. The old scar on his left cheek remained, as if even in sleep he had found no peace. Liang Hu placed a cleaned short knife in the corner of the table, its edge polished bright.
“He sharpened it for me,” Liang Hu said.
Zhao An stood in the doorway. Manu could think of nothing comforting, so he laid down his own dried rations. Zhai Hei let his hands hang at his sides and did not look up for a long time.
Murong Shao came too. Liang Hu looked at him. “I didn’t kill him,” he said quietly.
“I know,” Murong Shao replied.
Neither found anything more to say. Two days earlier they might have traded insults over the knife. Now neither could open his mouth.

That night Fu Jian ordered the verified facts read out before the headquarters tent. Liang Hu’s knife had been stolen; Sun Fu was implicated and had received gold; another person had silenced him after the murder. The man who paid for it had not been found, and the horse dealer’s death remained under investigation. Fu Jian called for no acclamations and would not paper over the matter with the words “case closed.” He ordered military magistrates to be appointed jointly by the Secretariat, central command, and the Court of Justice; autopsies, arrests, and testimony were to bear signatures from all three offices. The commander and deputy commander received reprimands for allowing the camp to come close to mutiny. Fu Chong’s separate offense in bringing his old personal troops was entered as well.
Fu Chong listened with a face like iron. Murong Chui accepted the disciplinary order and asked only whether drills could proceed at the appointed hour the next morning. Fu Jian said they could.

At morning inspection, Zhao An read four names from the wooden tally. He paused at the fifth space, then wrote Helai Yan’s name there too. The roll clerk said the dead should be struck from the military register. Zhao An handed him the sheet. “Crossing him out belongs to the register. Our squad is a man short today. That belongs on the roll as well.”
The clerk studied him, then added: “Deceased; replacement pending.”

The drums sounded before the ranks. Liang Hu stood beside the empty place, still seeming to hear Helai Yan curse him for riding too fast. With an unmarked new knife in hand, he marched beneath the Qin banner.
The blood on the camp gateposts had been washed away. Something dark lingered deep in the grain of the wood.

Sunlight reached the central banner as a wind rose across the Guanzhong plain. The cloth unfurled, missing a corner torn away when the crowd surged together the previous night. A banner maker stood looking up and said it ought to be taken down and repaired. Murong Chui told him to wait until drill was over.
So the Qin banner, its corner missing, flew above thirty thousand men for another day.
